opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think the field hasn't fully caught up on. For a long time, we evaluated models as if there were a single number: you run the benchmark, you get a score, you put it in a table. That made sense when inference was roughly fixed cost. You ask a question, you get an answer, and the compute spent is about the same every time.

With reasoning models, that's no longer true. You can let a model think for a few seconds or for many minutes, and performance can keep climbing as you do. So reporting a single score without saying how much compute went into it is a bit like reporting a chess engine's strength without saying how long it got per move. The number on its own doesn't mean much.

What I'd like to see is evaluation as a curve rather than a point. Show performance as a function of test-time compute, or better yet, as a function of cost, because cost is ultimately what people care about. Then you can ask more meaningful questions. At a given budget, which model is better? How steeply does performance scale? Where does it plateau? Two models might look identical at low compute, but one keeps improving while the other flattens out, and that's a really important difference.

I also think it pushes us to think about the value of the task. For some problems, like a hard math proof, a new drug candidate, or a tricky bug in critical infrastructure, you'd happily pay a lot more for a better answer. For others, like a quick chat reply, you want it fast and cheap. So the right evaluation depends on where you are on that tradeoff, and benchmarks should make that tradeoff visible rather than hiding it.

The other piece is that as these models get stronger, a lot of our benchmarks saturate quickly. So you need evaluations that are genuinely hard and have room at the top, where more thinking time could plausibly translate into meaningfully better results. Otherwise you can't even see the scaling, because everything is pinned near a hundred percent.

So the short version is: stop treating it as one number. Treat it as a cost-performance frontier, and compare models along that frontier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says performance may plateau and recommends hard benchmarks with room at the top, but does not state that reaching saturation takes so much test-time compute that evaluation becomes impractical.

r002.rationale: It asks which model is better “at a given budget,” recommending comparison under a specified resource budget.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends showing performance as a function of test-time compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the way we've traditionally evaluated models kind of breaks down once test-time compute becomes a variable. Historically you'd take a model, run it on a benchmark, get a number, and that number was the capability of the model. That made sense when inference was basically fixed cost. You ask the question, you get the answer, done.

With reasoning models, the number depends heavily on how much the model is allowed to think. If you let o1 or o3 think for a second versus a minute versus an hour, you can get very different results. So a single number is almost meaningless unless you say what the compute budget was. The thing I'd push for is reporting a curve rather than a point. You plot accuracy against test-time compute, and that curve tells you a lot more than any individual score. It tells you where the model is at low budgets, it tells you how steeply it improves, and it tells you where it plateaus, if it plateaus at all.

And I think the slope of that curve is actually the interesting part. Two models might have the same accuracy at some fixed budget, but if one keeps improving as you give it more compute and the other flattens out, those are fundamentally different systems. The one that keeps scaling is far more valuable, because for the problems people actually care about, like hard math, hard science, hard engineering problems, you're willing to spend a lot of compute. Nobody cares if it takes a model ten minutes to prove a theorem that would take a human months.

The other thing I'd say is that benchmarks need to get harder, and they need to get harder faster than they have been. A lot of the standard evals are saturating, and once a benchmark is saturated it stops telling you anything about the scaling behavior. You can't see the curve if everything's at ninety-nine percent. So I think things like FrontierMath, or really hard competition problems, or open research-style problems where there isn't a clean answer key, those are where evaluation needs to go. Ideally you want problems where even with a huge compute budget the model is still not at a hundred percent, because that's where you can actually measure progress.

And then there's a fairness question that comes up a lot, which is, is it fair to compare a model that's thinking for an hour against a model that's answering instantly? My view is that it's fine as long as you're transparent about it. Cost matters. If I can get the same answer for a thousandth of the compute, that's a real advantage. But it's not an apples-to-apples capability comparison, and people should stop treating it like one. The right framing is, what's the best result you can get at a given cost, and how does that change as cost goes up.

Honestly, I think we're heading toward a world where the question "how good is this model" doesn't have a single answer anymore. It's more like asking how fast a car is. Well, on what road, with how much fuel? And I think that's fine. That's actually what progress looks like here. The models that are going to matter most are the ones where the answer keeps getting better the more you're willing to spend.

r001.rationale: The response says models may plateau and recommends unsaturated hard problems, but it does not state that plateaus occur only after compute amounts that make saturation impractical to evaluate.

r002.rationale: It recommends comparing results at a given cost and says the compute budget should be disclosed.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends plotting accuracy against test-time compute.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to evaluate them as a function of how much compute you’re giving them at test time. A single accuracy number doesn’t really tell the whole story anymore. You want to see a curve: if I give the model ten times more compute, how much better does it get? And how does that compare with another model at the same cost?

There’s also a practical question about latency. If you’re asking a simple question, you probably want an answer immediately. If you’re working on a difficult research problem, you might be happy to wait hours for a useful answer. Those are different settings, and an evaluation should make clear which one it’s measuring.

And we need tasks that are hard enough to expose those differences. If every model gets close to perfect with a small amount of compute, the benchmark won’t tell us much about whether spending more time reasoning actually helps. So I’d want to look at accuracy, cost, and latency together, across a range of genuinely difficult tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says difficult tasks should show whether more reasoning helps, but does not state that performance plateaus only after impractically large amounts of test-time compute.

r002.rationale: It recommends comparing models “at the same cost,” specifying a shared test-time resource budget for the comparison.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends plotting a curve showing how performance changes as test-time compute increases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to evaluate the whole curve, rather than just a single score. If a model gets more time to think, how much better does it get, and what does that improvement cost? You want to compare models at similar compute budgets, or similar latency and dollar costs, because those answer different practical questions.

And you need problems that are hard enough for that curve to be meaningful. If every model is getting close to 100 percent on a benchmark, you can’t really tell whether additional reasoning is helping. Ideally, you have tasks where you can verify the answer, but where finding that answer requires substantial work.

The other piece is being clear about the setup. Did the model produce one answer after thinking for a long time, or did it generate a hundred candidates and use some mechanism to select one? Both can be useful, but the selection mechanism and its cost are part of the system you’re evaluating. So I’d want to see performance as a function of the total resources used, rather than treating benchmark performance as a fixed property of the model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improvement with more thinking time and hard benchmarks, but does not say that reaching a performance plateau requires impractical amounts of test-time compute.

r002.rationale: It recommends comparing models at similar compute budgets, latency, or dollar costs.

r003.rationale: It recommends evaluating the whole curve and explicitly says to measure performance as a function of total resources used.
